title: Dose-dense AC → paclitaxel every 2 weeks

agents.name: Doxorubicin
agents.explanation: Doxorubicin interferes with enzymes and DNA processes needed for cell division. It can also affect heart muscle, so the team considers previous exposure and cardiac risk.
agents.watch: Report pain or burning at the infusion site immediately. New breathlessness or chest symptoms need prompt review. Red urine for a short time can be a drug-colour effect; pain, clots or persistent bleeding still need advice.
risks: Low counts, infection and mouth ulcers
Severe tissue injury if the infusion leaks

agents.name: Cyclophosphamide
agents.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the body and damages DNA. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but can also affect blood-cell production and reproductive tissues.
agents.watch: Use the prescribed anti-sickness and hydration plan. Report fever, painful urination or blood in the urine.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next next dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
risks: Hair loss, muscle or joint pain
Mouth, bowel, skin and nail effects

context_label: neoadjuvant or adjuvant high-risk breast cancer
purpose: Part of an individual breast cancer plan to reduce the risk of recurrence, and to shrink the cancer before surgery where that is the agreed setting.
schedule_summary: Four AC cycles 14 days apart, followed by four paclitaxel doses 14 days apart. Growth-factor support accompanies the dose-dense course.

phases_title: The phases and how they connect
phases_note: The treatment phase determines the medicines, supportive prescription and tests. A phase change does not reset previous drug exposure or cardiac monitoring.
timeline_note: These broad symptom bands are educational possibilities, not measured risk curves. Infusion days are the planned schedule; delays require a new clinical plan.
safety_note: Fever, shivers, sudden illness, severe breathing changes or chest pain need prompt assessment on any day.
teachback: Can you explain which medicines you are receiving now? What symptoms mean you should call urgently? Which blood tests, scans or heart checks come next, and who arranges them?
consent_support: Use this information to discuss the treatment goal, alternatives, phase changes, important risks and monitoring with your team. It supports the approved local consent process.
urgent_extra: Report new breathing symptoms, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, painful swollen limbs, unusual bleeding, or worsening numbness. Tell staff immediately about infusion-site pain or an allergic reaction.

support.title: The correct phase prescription
support.text: AC is high emetogenic risk; a separate low-risk taxane script replaces it.

support.title: Premedicines and growth factors
support.text: Paclitaxel premedicines differ between weekly and fortnightly dosing. Use the phase-specific prescription.

support.title: Tests and appointments
support.text: The team should name the booking owner, due window and person reviewing each required test. Tell them if an expected appointment has not arrived.

support.title: After chemotherapy
support.text: Discuss recovery, fertility, rehabilitation and the next treatment or surveillance step.

questions.a: Four AC cycles 14 days apart, followed by four paclitaxel doses 14 days apart. Growth-factor support accompanies the dose-dense course.

Baseline cardiac assessment before AC. Repeat imaging according to symptoms, anthracycline exposure and cardiac risk; no universal 12-week echo schedule is assigned to AC alone. ESC guidance supplements the source: baseline echo before anthracyclines; high / very-high cardiac risk may need echo every two cycles and within 3 months after treatment. Test timing follows the treatment, clinical findings and local pathway.

questions.q: Where do surgery and radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: Two possible pathways: neoadjuvant systemic treatment → surgery / pathology → postoperative plan; or surgery first → adjuvant systemic treatment → radiotherapy when indicated. HER2-only treatment, if prescribed, may overlap radiation / endocrine therapy under MDT review. These are alternatives, not two consecutive surgery courses.

questions.q: Do I need routine CT scans or tumour markers?
questions.a: Early breast follow-up uses planned breast imaging. Routine CT / PET, blood tumour markers or other distant-recurrence screening are not recommended without symptoms or a clinical indication. After local treatment: annual mammography of remaining breast tissue; additional imaging when indicated.

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. This regimen has no routine take-home infusion pump. A port is an access device; the team removes the needle after the visit when appropriate and arranges device removal separately.

questions.q: Who arranges the scans and tests?
questions.a: Your treating service should book the planned checks, review the results and explain any change. If an expected appointment is missing, contact the team; this map does not book tests or confirm that they have happened.

questions.q: Why might this treatment be selected for me?
questions.a: Dose-dense AC followed by paclitaxel gives the planned chemotherapy at two-week intervals with growth-factor support. It may suit selected higher-risk early breast cancer. Fitness, blood-count recovery, heart health and practical support matter; it is a schedule choice with additional monitoring.

items.title: Your treatment setting
items.text: neoadjuvant or adjuvant high-risk breast cancer

items.title: The sequence
items.text: Four AC cycles 14 days apart, followed by four paclitaxel doses 14 days apart. Growth-factor support accompanies the dose-dense course.

items.title: Alternatives and your priorities
items.text: Ask what alternatives fit your cancer, what the treatment aims to achieve, and how its practical demands fit your life. The team can discuss personal benefits and risks.

chapters.title: Checks across treatment
chapters.intro: Your team arranges, reviews and acts on tests; an overdue result needs follow-up.

items.title: Blood tests
items.text: Baseline FBC, kidney and liver tests; review before each AC cycle and each paclitaxel administration under the regimen and local testing plan.

items.title: Heart monitoring
items.text: ESC supplementary guidance: baseline echo before anthracycline treatment. High/very-high cardiac risk: echo every two anthracycline cycles (for example before cycles 3 and 5 when continuing), and within 3 months after completion. All adults: echo within 12 months after completion. Other repeat tests depend on risk, cumulative exposure and symptoms.

items.title: ECG
items.text: Baseline ECG in the NCCP anthracycline source; repeat for symptoms or clinical risk. An ECG does not replace an echo.

items.title: Cancer scans
items.text: For early breast cancer, breast imaging and clinical review follow the agreed pathway. Routine CT/PET scans and blood tumour markers are not used to look for distant recurrence when there are no symptoms or clinical concerns.

chapters.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and later treatment
chapters.intro: Adjuvant pathway: surgery → chemotherapy → radiotherapy if indicated. Neoadjuvant pathway, where this regimen is indicated: chemotherapy → surgery → selected postoperative treatment and radiotherapy. Lumpectomy versus mastectomy is a surgical/MDT decision.

items.title: Hormone-receptor-positive disease
items.text: Endocrine treatment is considered when appropriate for the cancer biology and setting. It has its own schedule and monitoring; it is not automatically part of this chemotherapy prescription.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: DEXA is linked to an aromatase inhibitor, ovarian suppression, treatment-induced menopause or other bone risk—not automatically to every chemotherapy course. The endocrine team confirms baseline testing and risk-based repeat scans.

items.title: Markers and follow-up
items.text: After local treatment, the team plans mammography of remaining breast tissue. A mastectomy side does not need routine mammography. Report new symptoms rather than waiting for a scan.

items.title: Genomic tests
items.text: Where appropriate, the MDT may discuss a validated genomic test to inform the chemotherapy decision. This regimen card does not calculate an Oncotype result or select treatment from a score.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Blood tests, relevant cardiac assessment, medicines review, fertility discussion and the consent conversation come first.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Staff check the line, give prescribed premedicines and treatment, and observe for reactions. Tell them immediately about burning, pain, rash or breathlessness.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: First visits can take longer because of loading doses, premedicines and observation. Ask the unit about expected time, transport and any escort needed after sedation or line insertion.

details.title: Phase-specific visit pattern
details.text: Infusion and observation times differ by drug and first versus later doses; the unit confirms the full visit duration, including blood review and preparation.
